title: Hiring and job separation rates in the era of generative artificial intelligence: Early evidence
key_claim: Youth (15-29) hiring rates fell in every AI-exposure group between the six months to November 2022 and the six months to August 2026, most steeply in less-exposed occupations (4.0% to 3.3%), against 2.9% to 2.5% in augmentation-amenable jobs and 3.2% to 3.0% in substitution-prone jobs; coding-intensive jobs fell from 2.5% to 1.9%; separation rates were broadly flat.
frame_summary: Argues that, measured by worker flows, there is no broad evidence AI has cut hiring or raised separations in Canada so far, even for young workers; the decline looks like general cooling.

title: Young people not in education, employment or training (NEET), UK: August 2026
key_claim: An estimated 981,000 UK 16 to 24 year olds were NEET in April to June 2026, 13.0% of the age group, up 30,000 on a year earlier. Next release 26 November 2026.
frame_summary: Official statistics showing the UK youth disengagement stock still rising year on year, the UK counterpart to falling youth hiring flows.
verbatim_quote: There were an estimated 981,000 young people aged 16 to 24 years in the UK who were NEET in April to June 2026

The percentage of all young people in the UK who were NEET in April to June 2026 was 13.0%
notes: Stock measure, not flows. Down 30,000 on January to March 2026, so presented as a rise on the year only. title: No Widespread Displacement, but the AI Employment Gap for Young Workers Has Widened to 19%
key_claim: Using ADP payroll data, employment of 22 to 25 year olds in highly AI-exposed occupations is about 19% below its counterfactual as of June 2026, up from 15% at the July 2025 vintage; the same age group grew about 10% in the three least-exposed quintiles, and experienced workers show no comparable gap.
frame_summary: The strongest counter-position: argues there is no economy-wide displacement, but that an AI-specific gap for early-career workers in exposed jobs is real and widening.
verbatim_quote: by this same measure, the shortfall was 15% at the July 2025 data vintage and is 19% as of June 2026.
verbatim_list: employment of the same age group in the three least-exposed quintiles grew about 10%.
Experienced workers show no comparable gap.
notes: Counter-evidence source and the single structural anchor (3-6 month band). Authors Brynjolfsson, Chandar, Chen. US-only ADP data. title: What's behind young workers' job struggles?
key_claim: Employment of 22 to 26 year old graduates in high-AI-exposure occupations is only modestly below trend; the bigger shortfall is in medium-exposure occupations and began before ChatGPT; AI-beneficiary employers have outhired AI-agnostic employers since ChatGPT, with the largest net advantage among workers aged 22 to 26. Based on roughly 800 occupations.
frame_summary: Argues AI is not the main cause of graduates' job struggles; a low-fire, low-hire market is, and AI-adopting firms are hiring more young workers.
verbatim_quote: The bigger shortfall shows up in occupations with medium AI exposure
verbatim_list: Instead, since the release of ChatGPT, AI-beneficiary employers have outhired AI-agnostic employers overall.

title: Still waters, rapid currents: Early labor market transformation under generative AI
key_claim: Survey of 25,000 Danish workers in 11 highly AI-exposed occupations linked to administrative records rules out average earnings or hours effects larger than 2%; AI-exposed occupations have lost early-career jobs, but adopting firms are not driving that trend.
frame_summary: Argues AI is reorganising tasks beneath an unchanged surface, and that aggregate early-career declines should not be attributed to AI without measuring actual adoption.
verbatim_quote: but our data show that firms adopting generative AI are not driving these trends
verbatim_list: AI-exposed occupations have seen falls in early-career jobs
We surveyed 25,000 Danish workers in 11 occupations highly exposed to AI
notes: Authors Anders Humlum and Emilie Vestergaard. Administrative records run to December 2024. title: Jobs drought continues as vacancies fall
key_claim: 715,000 UK 16 to 24 year olds are unemployed, 54,000 more than a year earlier; vacancies are at 691,000, the lowest outside the pandemic since 2014; Work Foundation research shows adverts for starter jobs have almost halved.
frame_summary: Argues the UK has a demand-side jobs drought that shuts young people out before they start, and calls for direct job creation rather than placements and incentives.
verbatim_quote: In particular, there are now 715,000 young people aged 16–24 unemployed, down by 28,000 on the quarter.
verbatim_list: the number of young people out of work remains 54,000 higher than 12 months ago.
Overall, vacancies have fallen to 691,000 – the lowest level outside the pandemic since 2014 –
while Work Foundation research shows that adverts for starter jobs have almost halved over the past.
notes: Author Ben Harrison, Director. University think tank commentary on ONS data; starter-jobs claim treated directionally. title: Little evidence AI is to blame for decline in youth hiring, new StatCan study finds
key_claim: Canadian Press report of the StatCan study; Viet Vu of The Dais at Toronto Metropolitan University says AI's impact on the Canadian labour market cannot be detected yet, while the study author says AI is reshaping workflows.
frame_summary: Wire report framing the StatCan finding as undercutting AI-blame for youth hiring, while the study author stresses that AI is still reshaping workflows.
